extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (students and researchers) interested in examples of excellent mathematical writing and people contributing recommendations
extracted.subtask_description: A crowdsourced curated list of 'great' mathematics articles and books, with lightweight submission rules and guidance about what kinds of recommendations are appropriate. Contributors are asked to justify suggestions with personal/impactful reasons rather than generic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recommending works with major flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not propose writing that has a major flaw unless it is outweighed by some other truly outstanding qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explicitly asks contributors not to suggest items that contain major flaws unless exceptional merits compensate. No strict definition of 'major flaw' is given; use contributor judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish great exposition from great theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: "Great writing" is not the same as "proof of a great theorem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations should reflect excellence in exposition/communication/insight, not merely the importance of the mathematical result proved in the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: No self-recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: You are not allowed to recommend anything by yourself or the page author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is intended to avoid self-promotion; the author notes both they and the contributor should not list their own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit recommendations per contributor
rubrics_metrics.description: No more than three recommendations per person, please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors should cap submissions at three items to keep the list manageable and diverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicates allowed (multiplicity counted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feel free to pick things already on this list so they will appear with multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page will keep track of how many times each item is proposed; contributors may repeat existing entries to register support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give substantive, personal reasons for recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reasons that convey personal impact or concrete influence rather than vague claims of general quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable reason examples: 'This paper changed my life.'; 'This book inspired me to become a topologist.'; 'Anyone in my field who hasn't read this paper has led an impoverished existence.'; 'I wish someone had told me about this paper when I was younger.' Unacceptable examples: 'This paper is really very good.'; 'This book is the only book covering this material in a reasonable way.'; 'This is the best article on this subject.' The page asks for specific, vivid endorsement rather than bland or purely utility-based statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of eligible works
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible items: undergraduate texts and up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is intended for works at undergraduate level or higher; elementary or pre-undergraduate items are implicitly out of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curatorial anonymity and multiplicity handling
rubrics_metrics.description: The page will not attach contributor names to suggestions but will track the number of times each work is proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors' suggestions are anonymized on the page; popularity is reflected by multiplicity counts rather than by named endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-canonical, subject-weighted sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: The list is informal, arbitrary, and will be biased toward the tastes of contributors (not a community canonical list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns readers that the list will be weighted toward algebraic geometry and should be read as a sampling of tastes rather than an authoritative community verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: No prescriptive master-criteria provided
rubrics_metrics.description: The page's author explicitly refuses to provide a formal definition or fixed criteria for 'greatness'; contributors must exercise their own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than a checklist, contributors are expected to justify choices subjectively; the page provides examples of acceptable vs unacceptable justifications but no formal scoring rubric.
